strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: optimizing generators jointly with downstream safety filters (compound systems) rather than in isolation is a relevant and under-explored deployment setting.

The decision-theoretic framing (Section 3, Eq. 1-2, Proposition 1) is simple and transparent, and gives a clean intuition for why boundary-avoiding rewards are preferable to pure rejection-probability minimization.
Solid experimental breadth: four policy models across scales (0.5B-14B) and two architectures (Qwen2.5, Gemma-2), with a realistic training stack (GRPO + LoRA + Llama Guard 2 + Skywork reward model).

Informative ablations: the guard-only ablation shows the reward model is dispensable for larger models, and the prompt-aware ablation is a genuinely instructive negative result (deliberately generating confidently-unsafe content backfires), with failure mechanisms analyzed in the appendix.

Statistical testing (weighted paired t-tests on per-prompt differences), honest reporting of the Qwen-14B helpfulness regression, a reasonable limitations section, an ethics statement, and disclosure of LLM assistance.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim — that Boundary Guidance reduces false positives and false negatives of the filter — is never directly measured. The paper claims FP/FN reduction (Figure 1, Section 7) but evaluates only via GPT-4.1 helpfulness/harmfulness scores. Reporting actual filter FP/FN rates on benign and harmful test sets would substantially strengthen the causal story connecting the theory to the results.

Evaluation relies on a single LLM judge (GPT-4.1) with no human evaluation, no agreement analysis with human raters, and no validation that the judge's harm scores are reliable (e.g., against Llama Guard labels). Since the harm metric is the primary outcome, this is a significant soundness concern.

The reproduction statement is incomplete: 'Code available at' is followed by nothing (no URL). For a paper whose contribution is a fine-tuning recipe, this materially weakens reproducibility; KL coefficient values, number of seeds/runs, and variance across runs are also not reported, suggesting single-run experiments.

The theoretical contribution is thin: Proposition 1 is elementary calculus on a piecewise-linear function, and the constant-utility assumption (u ≡ u̅) that makes it work is strong and acknowledged only implicitly.

Practical rewards are inconsistent with the theory in a potentially exploitable way: Eq. 3 rewards higher unsafe probability t(x,y) when t ≥ 0.5, exactly the failure mode the paper's own prompt-aware ablation demonstrates (Appendix C shows harmful unfiltered completions). The paper does not explain why the main reward avoids this gaming, nor whether classifier calibration (a stated assumption in Section 7.2) holds for Llama Guard 2 logits.

Evidence of improvement is concentrated in the smallest model: helpfulness gains for Qwen-7B are not significant, helpfulness drops (insignificantly) for Qwen-14B, so the 'Pareto improvement' claim is driven mostly by one weak base model and one modest Gemma result.

Training/test data come from the same distributions and jailbreak families; no evaluation on out-of-distribution harm categories or adaptive attacks, limiting claims of robustness. Max completion length of 96 tokens during training may also explain the small-model refusal collapse and constrains generality.

strengths: The core observation is intuitive and well-motivated: fine-tuning generators against a downstream filter can push outputs toward the classifier's decision boundary, and a simple decision-theoretic model (Section 3) cleanly illustrates why expected utility is minimized near the threshold.

The method is simple and practical: the boundary-avoiding reward (Eq. 3) requires only classifier logits plus an optional reward model, and is implemented with standard tools (GRPO + LoRA) on public models.

Experiments cover multiple model scales (0.5B–14B) and two architectures, with paired statistical tests and useful ablations; the prompt-aware reward ablation (Section 6.2.2) is an interesting negative result showing that deliberately generating 'confidently unsafe' content backfires.
Limitations and dual-use considerations are discussed honestly (Section 7.1, Ethics Statement).
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is not directly measured. The paper claims Boundary Guidance 'reduces false positives and false negatives' and improves the compound system, but the main results (Table 1, Figure 2) only report LLM-judged helpfulness/harmfulness of the generator; false positive/negative filtering rates of the compound system are reported only for the failing prompt-aware ablation (Table 5), not for the main method. The filter-level behavior — the actual point of the paper — is never evaluated for the proposed reward.

No baselines. The method is compared only against the un-fine-tuned base model. There is no comparison against existing safety fine-tuning approaches (Safe RLHF, C-DPO, SafeDPO, SACPO, safe-completions), all of which are discussed in Section 2, so it is impossible to judge whether the compound-system framing yields benefits that simpler standalone safety training would not.

The theoretical contribution is thin. Proposition 1 is an immediate property of a piecewise-linear function, and the connection between theory and practice is loose: the theory's threshold τ and λ are never used, the implemented reward arbitrarily replaces τ with 0.5, and the reward model term u(x,y) is claimed theoretically necessary yet the guard-only ablation (Section 6.2.1) shows it is unnecessary for three of four models — directly undercutting the theoretical motivation.

Evaluation rests entirely on a single LLM judge (GPT-4.1) with prompts adapted from Yuan et al. (2025); there is no human evaluation, no agreement analysis, no standard safety benchmark, and judge scores are on narrow scales (1–4 helpful, 0–3 harmful). Given the small effect sizes (e.g., Δhelp of +0.03), judge reliability is a material concern.

Empirical gains are mixed and modest: helpfulness improves significantly in only two of four models, decreases (insignificantly) for Qwen2.5-14B, and the largest gains occur on the smallest model, which has unclear practical relevance.

Reproducibility is compromised: the Reproducibility statement ends with 'Code available at' followed by no URL, so no code is actually provided. Several hyperparameters (KL coefficient, group settings beyond generations per step) are also not reported.

The paper reads as rushed: typos and contradictions such as 'which hence does require additional computation at inference time' (should be 'does not', Section 7.1), 'derives negative 1 utility' (Section 3), and uncited in-text references ('Llama Team (2024)', 'Qwen et al., 2025').

Methodological details raise concerns: rollouts are capped at 96 tokens, which may not represent realistic deployments; the calibration of Llama Guard 2 logits (assumed by the whole approach) is never validated; and test prompts are drawn from the same narrow dataset distribution as training.
